target_customer: Creators, influencers and organizations selling made-to-order merchandise to their audience, and their fans
problem: Selling custom merchandise required upfront inventory. Teespring let anyone launch a campaign, collect orders and have the product printed only if a minimum was met.
business_model: Marketplace take on each sale of print on demand products

competitors.name: Kickstarter
competitors.what: Crowdfunding platform; early press framed Teespring as a Kickstarter for t-shirts

technical_complexity.rationale: Campaign pages, payments and order batching with a print partner; operations and fulfillment mattered more than software.

defensibility.rationale: A seller base and Facebook driven traffic helped, but print on demand was copyable and later rivals competed on price.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent bought it; competition and dependence on Facebook eroded growth and it was sold to Amaze in 2022.

market_need_then: Creators and groups wanted merch with no upfront cost. A bar saving shirt sold over 400 units from a one page site in 2011, and a source reports 750,000 dollars monthly revenue in March 2013.

branding.domain_note: Used teespring.com; it now redirects to an Amaze page.
branding.brand_signature: The first FREE FISHCO shirt campaign

rebrands.why: CEO Chris Lamontagne said it signaled a vision beyond tees as architecture for creator commerce; one review notes over 180 products and distance from just tees.

branding.community_and_virality: Hundreds of thousands of creators used it per Tubefilter (450,000), with heavy YouTuber merch use; Business Insider covered customer frustration after the rebrand.

brand_strength.rationale: Teespring became a default word for creator merch with hundreds of thousands of sellers, though the 2021 rebrand coincided with trouble.

pivots.from: Jobzle, an internship site for students
pivots.why: The FREE FISHCO shirt sold over 400 units and drew requests from other groups

outcome_analysis: Teespring grew fast, raising 55M by 2014 on a 615M reported valuation, but cut staff repeatedly from 2015, shut its Rhode Island operation and in 2017 recapitalized in a round valuing it far lower. Crunchbase News tied the revenue decline mainly to dependence on Facebook for sales and the departure of power sellers. It reached profitability by 2019 and rebranded as Spring in 2021, then was acquired by Amaze in November 2022; reports of a later shutdown are unverified.
notes: Seed and Series A amounts come from Wikipedia only; Series B and recap are from Crunchbase News (Pitchbook 615M, other source 611M). The 2017 recap valuation near 30.8M was unconfirmed and is not recorded. Wikipedia reports dissolution on 2026-09-15, needs news sources, not recorded. The YC round of 1.3M in Dec 2013 is not recorded as a round. Batch listed as Winter 2013 by the directory while Wikipedia says Dec 2013 acceptance.
